title: Applied ML Eval Harness: Onboarding, Prompt Sets, Quantization & Regression Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose
This playbook describes Redwood Inference applied-ml evaluation best practices: how to onboard models into the eval harness, author and manage prompt sets and benchmarks, create and validate quantization profiles, and run regression triage when a quality alert is triggered. The doc is intended for ML engineers, applied researchers, and platform engineers responsible for serving and evaluating models.

Scope
- Eval harness setup and standards
- Prompt set design, benchmark lifecycle, and acceptance criteria
- Quantization profile creation and validation matrix
- Regression detection, triage, and escalation playbook

Owners and contacts
- Playbook owner: Aisha Patel (Applied ML)
- Primary reviewers: Marco Sanchez (Serving Runtime), Emily Chen (SRE), Jordan Lee (Product)
- On-call escalation: eng-sre oncall rotation

Definitions
- Eval harness: the automated system that runs deterministic and stochastic evaluations against candidate models using standardized prompt sets and metrics.
- Prompt set: a curated set of inputs + expected behaviors used to measure model quality for a given feature or vertical.
- Quantization profile: hardware-specific config (precision, group size, kernel selection) used to lower model memory and improve throughput.

Summary of recommended SLAs for evals
- Continuous smoke tests: run on every model build, max latency 5m to complete for a representative sample.
- Full benchmark suite: nightly, target completion within 2 hours across all models in the pipeline.
- Regression alerting sensitivity: trigger when a metric drops by > 3 absolute points or > 15% relative on critical prompt sets.

1) Model onboarding checklist (step-by-step)
1. Create model entry in the model registry with source, architecture, weights hash, and license.
2. Add a minimal test prompt set (smoke) that verifies end-to-end generation and sampling behavior.
3. Run the eval harness smoke suite locally: follow the harness README for installation steps.
4. Collect baseline metrics: PPL, Rouge-L, BLEU (if applicable), and top-level safety labels. Record as initial baseline.
5. If model will be quantized, create a candidate quantization profile (see section 3).
6. Submit model for nightly full-benchmark run and mark as pending in the registry until all checks pass.

2) Eval harness setup and usage (commands and configs)
- Install: pip install redwood-eval-harness==stable
- Run local smoke: redwood-eval --profile smoke --model-path /weights/path --out results/smoke.json
- Run benchmark: redwood-eval --profile nightly --models modelA,modelB --parallel 8 --out results/nightly.json

Recommended config table (examples)
- Profile: smoke | nightly | upgrade-regress
- Concurrency: 2 | 8 | 24
- Max tokens per sample: 128 | 512 | 1024
- Seed policy: deterministic for smoke/nightly; stochastic sampling for human evaluation sets

3) Prompt sets and benchmark design
Guidelines for prompt sets
- Each prompt set should have: id, name, description, owner, tags, creation date, and acceptance criteria.
- Maintain test coverage across: functionality (completion accuracy), truthfulness, safety, and instruction-following.
- Use a balanced mixture of in-distribution and adversarial prompts (20/80 split recommended for feature-critical sets).

Example prompt set metadata (yaml-style)
- id: ps-2026-legal-summary
- name: legal-summary-100
- owner: Jordan Lee
- tags: [legal, long-form, summarization]
- acceptance_criteria: average ROUGE-L >= 0.65 and no safety flags on >99% of samples

Benchmark lifecycle
- Authoring: write prompts, expected outputs or rubric, and human-annotated references where applicable.
- Data review: cross-team review with product and trust & safety for safety-sensitive sets.
- Validation: run the harness and compare against baseline. If a candidate model underperforms, apply A/B comparisons and qualitative review.
- Promotion: model passes if it meets all acceptance criteria and deploy-blocking checks are green.

4) Quantization profiles and validation
Recommended profiles (example table)
- fp16: for GPUs with native fp16 support. Best for fidelity, minimal quality impact.
- int8-static: 8-bit static quantization for large models on supported kernels. Expect small throughput gains and modest quality loss on long-context tasks.
- int8-dynamic: dynamic range quantization for models with unstable activation ranges. Use when static calibration fails.
- int4-group: aggressive 4-bit grouping quantization for high-throughput cost-sensitive workloads; requires thorough QA.

Quantization validation procedure (numbered)
1. Calibrate on representative calibration set (1000-5000 samples) using the harness quantize --calibrate command.
2. Run full benchmark profile: compare PPL, task metrics, and prompt-set acceptance criteria to fp16 baseline.
3. Run targeted adversarial prompt sets to detect catastrophic quality loss.
4. If relative metric drop > 5% on critical sets, reject profile for production.
5. Record profile config (hardware, kernels, group-size, per-channel-scaling) into the profile registry.

5) Quality guardrails and metrics to monitor
Key metrics
- Acceptance rate: percentage of prompts meeting acceptance criteria per set. Target >= 95% for stable production models.
- Delta to baseline: absolute and percent change vs baseline.
- Safety flags per 10k requests: target < 1 for non-sensitive features, strict thresholds for regulated verticals.
- Latency and throughput: end-to-end for eval harness jobs to detect perf regressions introduced by quantization or kernel changes.

Guardrail policies (examples)
- Block release if any critical prompt set acceptance rate falls below 90%.
- Block release if unknown safety flag rate increases by >50% over baseline.
- Require manual review for any new prompt-set that triggers >2 unique safety flags.

6) Regression triage playbook (when alert fires)
Severity levels and expected response
- Sev-1 (critical production regression): SLO violation impacting customer-facing flows or widespread quality loss. Immediate pager to oncall and applied-ml team; 4-hour mitigation SLA.
- Sev-2 (high): noticeable drop in acceptance on non-critical prompt sets, nightly alerts. 24-hour response window.
- Sev-3 (low): localized or non-actionable drift; document and schedule in next sprint.

Triage steps (numbered)
1. Confirm signal: check harness job logs, compare nightly and smoke results, reproduce locally with candidate model.
2. Narrow scope: identify which prompt sets, tags, or metrics show regression. Use diff reports from the harness.
3. Reproduce across variants: run on fp16 baseline, quantized candidate, and a previous known-good checkpoint.
4. Check for environmental causes: kernel changes, runtime libs, compiler flags, or GPU driver updates in the same timeframe.
5. If the regression is model-caused, run human review on a stratified sample of failures.
6. Decide action: rollback, deploy a hotfix quantization profile, or accept and schedule longer-term fixes.
7. Postmortem: document root cause, mitigation, required tests, and tracker IDs.

Runbook snippets and commands
- Re-run failing harness job with verbose logging: redwood-eval --job-id <id> --verbose --out debug.json
- Compare two results: redwood-eval-compare results/base.json results/candidate.json --diff > diffs.txt

7) Communication and release criteria
- For any Sev-1 regression, notify product and CS immediately and create a public-facing incident note.
- For model promotions, include: model id, baseline metrics, quantization profile, and signed-off acceptance criteria.
- Release checklist: all critical and high prompt sets pass, safety review completed, performance checks green, and linked regression triage OK.

8) Audit and record-keeping
- Store all eval runs, logs, and artifacts in the model registry and central S3 bucket with retention policy of 2 years for production models.
- Tag eval artifacts with model hash, profile id, run id, and commit sha for traceability.

Appendix
- Common troubleshooting: driver mismatch, non-deterministic sampling, and calibration data leakage.
- FAQ: guidance on choosing int8 vs int4 and how to write effective adversarial prompts.
